entries.text: A multiplexer picks one of many inputs and sends it to a single output. This lesson is about the blocks that go the other way, and about their mirror images. A decoder takes an n-bit number and turns on exactly one of 2^n output lines: the one whose index is that number. A demultiplexer takes one data bit and steers it onto one of 2^n output lines. An encoder does the reverse of a decoder: it looks at 2^n lines, one of which is on, and reports the index of that line as an n-bit code. A priority encoder is an encoder that still behaves sensibly when several lines are on at once: it reports the most important one. Along the way we will see that a decoder is a complete minterm generator (so a decoder and one OR gate can build any function), how to build a big decoder out of small ones, and how decoders select one word of a memory, which is where GATE most often meets them. Where this fits Lesson 2 built functions from multiplexers, and the MUX equation Y = \sum_i m_i(S)\, I_i already contained every minterm of the select lines. A decoder is that set of minterms on its own, one per wire. The minterms themselves come from Chapter 2, Lesson 4. A decoder followed by a programmable OR array is a ROM, which Lesson 5 studies. Memory addressing (how many address bits a memory needs) comes back in the computer-organisation part of the syllabus; here we only need the decoder's side of it. Decoders: one line on for each input number Picture the panel behind a hotel reception desk with one small lamp for every room. The receptionist types a room number, and exactly one lamp lights: the lamp of that room. Typing 5 lights lamp 5 and nothing else; typing 6 moves the light to lamp 6. The panel never lights two lamps at once and never lights none (while it is switched on). A decoder is that panel in logic. Its address inputs carry a binary number; its outputs are numbered 0, 1, \dots, 2^n - 1; the output whose number equals the address is 1 and every other output is 0. A master switch, the enable, can turn the whole panel off, and then every lamp is dark. The interesting part is what the lamps are: lamp i is lit on exactly one input row, row i, so it is the minterm m_i. A decoder hands you every minterm of its inputs on a separate wire. An n:2^n decoder (also written n-to-2^n or n \times 2^n) has n address inputs A_{n-1} \dots A_1 A_0 (with A_{n-1} the most significant bit), usually one enable input E, and 2^n outputs D_0, \dots, D_{2^n - 1}. Active-high outputs (the default): when E = 1, the output D_i whose index i equals the address (A_{n-1} \dots A_0)_2 is 1 and all other outputs are 0. The outputs are one-hot: exactly one of them is 1. When E = 0 every output is 0. Active-low outputs: every output is inverted. When enabled, the selected output is 0 and all the others are 1 (one-cold); when disabled, every output is 1. The pins are usually drawn with a bubble and named \overline{D}_i. Active-low enable: the enable pin has a bubble and the decoder works when \overline{E} = 0. A 2:4 decoder with enable is four 3-input AND gates and two inverters: D_0 = E\,\overline{A_1}\,\overline{A_0}, D_1 = E\,\overline{A_1}A_0, D_2 = E\,A_1\overline{A_0}, D_3 = E\,A_1A_0. A 3:8 decoder has eight 4-input ANDs, and so on. The decoder has no select lines and no data input: the address bits are its only information inputs. Some decoders use fewer than 2^n outputs: a BCD-to-decimal decoder has 4 inputs and only 10 outputs (the codes 10–15 never occur). For an n:2^n decoder with active-high outputs and enable E, D_i = E \cdot m_i(A_{n-1}, \dots, A_0) \qquad (i = 0, 1, \dots, 2^n - 1), where m_i is the i-th minterm of the address variables, with A_{n-1} as the most significant bit. With active-low outputs, \overline{D}_i = \overline{E \cdot m_i}, which for E = 1 is the maxterm M_i. Idea first: both sides are 1 on exactly the same input rows, namely row i with the enable on. By definition, D_i = 1 exactly when E = 1 and the address bits read i in binary. The minterm m_i is the product of all n address literals, each in the polarity of the corresponding bit of i (plain where the bit is 1, complemented where it is 0), so m_i = 1 exactly when the address bits read i. Hence E \cdot m_i = 1 exactly when E = 1 and the address is i: the same rows. Two Boolean functions that are 1 on the same rows are equal. For active-low outputs, complement both sides; with E = 1, \overline{m_i} = M_i by De Morgan. Turn the hotel panel inside out: every lamp is normally on, and typing a room number makes that one lamp go dark. The panel carries exactly the same information (one lamp differs from all the others, and its position is the number you typed), only the polarity is reversed. Someone who looks for "the lit lamp" on this panel sees seven lit lamps and is confused; someone who looks for "the odd lamp out" reads it at once. That is an active-low decoder. Its selected output is the one that is 0. Because every output is now the complement of a minterm, the gate that collects them must change too: where an active-high decoder needs an OR ("is any of my lamps lit?"), an active-low one needs a NAND ("is any of my lamps dark?"). The rest of this block makes that precise. Real decoder chips usually have active-low outputs, because a NAND gate is cheaper than an AND gate. The selected output goes to 0 and the rest stay at 1. By the theorem above, with the enable on, \overline{D}_i = \overline{m_i} = M_i: the active-low outputs are the maxterms of the address. That changes which gate builds a function: Active-high outputs are minterms, so f = \text{OR} of the outputs of f's 1-rows. Active-low outputs are complemented minterms, so f = \text{NAND} of the outputs of f's 1-rows (\overline{\overline{m_a}\,\overline{m_b}\cdots} = m_a + m_b + \cdots by De Morgan), or f = \text{AND} of the outputs of f's 0-rows (a product of maxterms is the canonical POS). So a NAND gate on an active-low decoder plays the role of the OR gate on an active-high decoder, and an A

entries.title: Magnitude comparators and parity circuits
headings: Comparing two numbers: the first difference decides
Cascading comparators and counting their gates
entries.text: Two circuits in this lesson answer two of the most common questions a computer asks about bits. A magnitude comparator answers "which of these two numbers is bigger?", and a parity circuit answers "has any bit of this word been flipped?". Both look like simple gate puzzles, and both rest on one clean idea each. For the comparator the idea is that numbers compare like words in a dictionary: the first place they differ settles everything. For parity it is that an XOR of many bits only cares whether the number of 1s is odd. We prove both ideas, build the circuits, count their gates, chain small comparators into big ones, and see exactly which errors parity can and cannot catch. Where this fits Lesson 1 gave the design procedure (specification → truth table → minimal expression → gates); here we run it on two classic specifications. The XOR and XNOR laws come from Chapter 2, Lesson 3, which already proved that an n-input XOR computes odd parity; parity bits as a code were introduced in Chapter 1, Lesson 8. Comparing numbers by subtracting them is arithmetic, taught in Chapter 1, Lesson 9; the adder–subtractor circuit was built in Chapter 4 (arithmetic circuits). This lesson only shows how the borrow and the zero test turn that subtractor into a comparator. Lesson 2 supplies the multiplexer on which the Live Lab realises a comparator. Comparing two numbers: the first difference decides To decide whether "carton" comes before "cartel" in a dictionary, you read both words from the left, skip the letters they share ("cart"), and stop at the first letter where they differ: "o" against "e"; "e" comes first in the alphabet, so "cartel" comes before "carton". That one letter decides the order, and nothing after it matters ("n" against "l" is never looked at). Binary numbers of the same length work exactly the same way, with the most significant bit (MSB) playing the role of the first letter. Compare A = 1010 and B = 1001: the first two bits agree (1 and 1, then 0 and 0); the third bit is the first difference, and there A has the 1. So A > B, whatever the last bits say. Indeed the last bits point the other way (A_0 = 0, B_0 = 1), and they are simply outvoted: the bit where the numbers first differ is worth more than all the bits below it put together. A comparator circuit is this reading procedure turned into gates: one small test per bit ("are these two bits equal?"), and a rule that lets a bit speak only when every bit above it has said "equal". A magnitude comparator for n-bit unsigned numbers A and B has three outputs: G (A > B), E (A = B) and L (A < B). For one bit the truth table has four rows: Reading each column as a sum of its rows: G = AB', \qquad E = A'B' + AB = A \odot B = (A \oplus B)', \qquad L = A'B . On every row exactly one of G, E, L is 1, because exactly one of the three relations holds between two numbers. So any one output can be made from the other two: E = (G + L)', a NOR. Gate cost with only uncomplemented inputs: two inverters, two ANDs (G, L) and one NOR for E (or an XNOR on A, B). An all-NOR version needs only four NOR gates and no inverters: let N = (A + B)'; then (A + N)' = A'B = L, (B + N)' = AB' = G and (G + L)' = E. Two words are the same word only if they agree letter by letter, in every position. For bits that is a chain of "and": bit 3 agrees and bit 2 agrees and … and bit 0 agrees. The per-bit agreement test is the XNOR from the table above, because XNOR is 1 exactly when its two inputs are equal. So an equality comparator is a row of XNOR gates feeding one AND gate. For n-bit numbers write x_i = A_i \odot B_i = A_iB_i + A_i'B_i' (1 exactly when bit i of A equals bit i of B). Then E = (A = B) = x_{n-1}\,x_{n-2} \cdots x_1\,x_0 . Hardware: n XNOR gates and one n-input AND. With 2-input gates only, the AND becomes a tree of n - 1 two-input ANDs, so 2n - 1 gates in all. Equivalently E = \overline{(A_{n-1} \oplus B_{n-1}) + \dots + (A_0 \oplus B_0)}: n XORs and one NOR ("no bit differs"). The animation below builds this circuit for 4-bit numbers: a row of four XNORs, one per bit position, feeding one AND. A single unequal position is enough to make the AND output 0. For n-bit unsigned numbers, A = B as numbers if and only if A_i = B_i for every i, that is, if and only if x_{n-1} x_{n-2} \cdots x_0 = 1. Idea first: a binary number has only one way of being written in n bits, so equal values force equal bit patterns. If every bit agrees, then A = \sum A_i 2^i = \sum B_i 2^i = B. Conversely, suppose some bit differs, and let k be the highest such bit. The bits above k agree and cancel in A - B; bit k contributes \pm 2^k, and the lower bits together are worth at most 2^k - 1 (because 1 + 2 + \dots + 2^{k-1} = 2^k - 1). So |A - B| \ge 2^k - (2^k - 1) = 1, and A \ne B. (Equivalently: binary representation is unique, which is the place-value fact of Chapter 1.) So A = B exactly when every x_i = 1, which is exactly when their AND is 1. Now the harder output, G. Think of the bits as a committee that votes from the most senior member down. The MSB votes first: if A_{n-1} = 1 and B_{n-1} = 0, then A > B and the meeting is over. If the MSBs are equal, the MSB abstains and the next bit gets to vote, but only because the MSB abstained. Bit i can declare "A is bigger" only when all the bits above it are equal (every x_j = 1 for j > i) and bit i itself is A_i = 1, B_i = 0. Write one product term for each bit that could be the first difference, and OR them together. That sentence is the comparator. With x_i = A_i \odot B_i, for 4-bit numbers A_3A_2A_1A_0 and B_3B_2B_1B_0: \begin{aligned} G = (A > B) &= A_3B_3' + x_3\,A_2B_2' + x_3x_2\,A_1B_1' + x_3x_2x_1\,A_0B_0', \\ L = (A < B) &= A_3'B_3 + x_3\,A_2'B_2 + x_3x_2\,A_1'B_1 + x_3x_2x_1\,A_0'B_0, \\ E = (A = B) &= x_3x_2x_1x_0 . \end{aligned} In general, the term for bit k is \left(\prod_{j > k} x_j\right) A_k B_k': the equalities of all higher bits, then "A has the 1 here". L is the same with the roles of A and B swapped. For n bits each

entries.title: ROM, PLA and PAL as combinational logic
headings: ROM: a truth table you can wire in
Building a bigger ROM from smaller chips
PLA: build only the terms you need
PAL, and choosing between the three
entries.text: Every circuit so far was designed for one function: you minimised it, then wired gates (or a MUX, or a decoder) to match. This lesson meets three chips that are built before anyone knows the function. A ROM stores the whole truth table and looks the answer up. A PLA builds only the product terms you ask for and lets several outputs share them. A PAL builds product terms too, but each output has its own private set. GATE asks one thing about them again and again: how big must the ROM be to hold a given table (four questions, all about multipliers). Behind that one question sit two ideas worth learning properly: a ROM is a decoder plus an OR array, and the product of two n-bit numbers needs exactly 2n bits. Where this fits Lesson 3 proved that the outputs of an n:2^n decoder are the 2^n minterms, and that ORing the right outputs realises any function. A ROM is exactly that circuit with the OR connections left programmable, so this lesson is Lesson 3 made into a product. The PLA and PAL come from the other end: they are the two-level AND–OR circuits of Chapter 3, Lesson 4 printed as a grid, with the shared product terms of multi-output minimisation becoming shared rows. The arithmetic that fills a multiplier or adder table (how wide a sum or a product is) is in Chapter 1, Lesson 9; adder and multiplier circuits were built from gates in Chapter 4 (arithmetic circuits), and here we only count their inputs and outputs. ROM: a truth table you can wire in Imagine the truth table of a 3-input, 2-output function printed on a card: eight rows, each row a line of two answer bits. To use it you do not simplify anything. You read the input as a row number, put your finger on that row, and read the two bits across. A read-only memory is that card in silicon. The input bits are the address (the row number), a decoder puts its finger on exactly one row (one word line goes high), and the stored bits of that row appear on the outputs. The striking consequence: a ROM never needs minimisation. A function with 200 product terms and a function with one cost the same, because the ROM stores every row whether the expression is short or long. That is its strength (any function fits) and its weakness (it pays for every row, even rows that are don't-cares). A 2^n \times m ROM has n address inputs and m data outputs. Inside: an n:2^n decoder whose outputs (the word lines) are the 2^n minterms m_0, \dots, m_{2^n - 1} of the address. This is the AND plane; it is fixed (every minterm is always built); m OR gates, one per output (the bit lines), each with a possible connection to every word line. This is the OR plane; it is programmable: a connection at (word line i, output j) means "bit j of word i is 1". So a ROM has 2^n \cdot m programmable crosspoints, exactly one per bit it stores. The size of a ROM is written words × bits per word: 2^n \times m. Its total capacity is 2^n \cdot m bits. Programming follows the truth table row by row: wherever the table has a 1, keep the connection; wherever it has a 0, leave it open. In array drawings a cross (×) at a crosspoint marks a programmable connection that is made, a dot marks a fixed connection, and no mark means no connection. The decoder's job is the one Lesson 3 described: for every address exactly one word line is 1, and that line is the minterm of the address. Each OR gate then outputs 1 exactly when the active word line is one of the lines connected to it. That is all a ROM is, and it already explains why it can store any function at all. A 2^n \times m ROM can be programmed to realise any m Boolean functions f_1, \dots, f_m of its n address inputs, by connecting output j to word line i exactly when f_j(i) = 1. Conversely, the outputs of a ROM are always functions of the address alone: it is a combinational circuit. Idea first: the decoder supplies every minterm, and an OR of minterms is the canonical SOP, which every function has. By Lesson 3, word line i is the minterm m_i of the address: it is 1 on row i and 0 on every other row. Output j is the OR of the word lines connected to it, so with the programming above it equals \sum_{i : f_j(i) = 1} m_i, which is the canonical SOP of f_j from Chapter 2, Lesson 4. Every function has a canonical SOP, so every f_j can be realised, and the m outputs are programmed independently because they share only the word lines, which are read and never altered. Conversely, for a fixed program each output is an OR of minterms of the address, a function of the address and nothing else: no memory of earlier inputs, so the read path is combinational. The animation stores a 3-bit squarer: the address is a 3-bit number x, word x holds x^2, and there are six output columns Q_5 \dots Q_0 because the largest square, 7^2 = 49 = 110001_2, has six bits. So it is an 8 \times 6 ROM, 48 stored bits. Its last step points out that two of those six columns never need storing; why that is so is proved under "Sizing a ROM" below, so take it on trust for now. Any other table goes in the same way. Here is an 8 \times 2 ROM programmed with two other columns: the majority of three bits and their odd parity. (They are the carry and the sum of adding three bits, which Chapter 4 (arithmetic circuits) built from gates; a ROM does not care what the columns mean.) Notice that the stored bits are the truth table: the ROM's contents and the function's table are one and the same object. The F_1 OR gate has four connections (m_3, m_5, m_6, m_7) and the F_2 OR gate has four (m_1, m_2, m_4, m_7); the word line m_7 feeds both, which costs nothing extra because every word line is built anyway. Mask ROM: the connections are made when the chip is manufactured; economical only in volume. PROM (programmable ROM): shipped with every connection made (or none); the user programs it once by blowing fuses with current pulses. It cannot be changed afterwards. EPROM: erasable (traditionally by ultraviolet light) and reprogrammable. EEPROM and flash: erased electrically, in place. Al

entries.title: Stuck-at faults and test inputs
headings: Detecting a fault: activation and propagation
entries.text: A circuit that has been designed correctly can still be built wrongly. A wire can be broken, a transistor can be shorted, a gate output can be welded to the supply rail. When a chip comes off the production line, nobody can open it and look; all a tester can do is apply input patterns and watch the outputs. This lesson asks the testing questions GATE asks: what does a broken wire do to the logic, how many different breakages are possible, which input pattern exposes a given breakage, and why some breakages can never be seen at all. The answers rest on one simple model, the stuck-at fault, and one simple idea: a fault is visible only if an input excites it and the circuit carries the damage to the output. Where this fits Chapter 2, Lesson 6 taught you to evaluate a circuit line by line for a given input. Testing is the same evaluation done twice, once for the good circuit and once for a broken copy, and compared. The rules for getting a signal through a gate use the controlling values of Chapter 2, Lesson 1. You have already met a stuck output once: in Chapter 3, Lesson 1, GATE 1997 asked on how many rows an output stuck at 0 is wrong. And the redundant consensus term that Chapter 3, Lesson 4 added to cure a hazard comes back here as the classic line whose fault no test can find. The stuck-at fault model Imagine a light switch on the wall that is jammed in the ON position. You walk past it every day with the lamp on and notice nothing, because the lamp is on exactly when you want it on. You discover the fault only on the evening you try to switch the lamp off and it refuses. Two things had to happen: you had to try to set the switch to the value it is stuck away from, and you had to be looking at a lamp that actually depends on that switch. If the lamp were also wired through a second switch that happened to be open, you would see darkness either way and learn nothing. That is the whole of testing in one picture. A stuck line shows itself only when the input tries to drive it to the other value (we call this activation), and only if the rest of the circuit lets that line decide the output (we call this propagation). Everything in this lesson is a careful version of those two sentences. A line is any wire of the circuit that can carry its own value: a primary input, a gate output, and each branch of a wire that fans out to several gates (the wire before the split is the stem). A line has a stuck-at-0 fault (s-a-0) if it is permanently 0, whatever drives it; it has a stuck-at-1 fault (s-a-1) if it is permanently 1. Everything downstream reads the stuck value; the gates themselves still work. A single stuck-at fault is one line stuck at one value, all other lines healthy. This is the model used to generate tests in practice, because it is simple and because tests for single faults catch most real defects. A multiple stuck-at fault is any non-empty set of lines, each stuck at a value of its own, all other lines healthy. The model is logical, not physical. A broken wire, a short to ground or a short to the supply each behave, at the level of 0s and 1s, like some line stuck at a constant, so one model covers many physical defects. (Which value a given short or open produces depends on the technology; the model does not care.) Two remarks before we count. First, a fan-out stem and its branches are different lines: if input A feeds two gates, a break in the branch to the first gate leaves the second gate reading the true A, which is a different fault from a break before the split. Second, the faulty circuit is still a combinational circuit; it simply computes a different function, and testing is about finding an input on which the two functions differ. Picture each line of the circuit as a dial with three positions: working, stuck at 0, stuck at 1. The good circuit is the one setting with every dial on "working". Any other setting of the dials is some fault. A single fault turns exactly one dial away from "working"; a multiple fault turns any number of them. Counting faults is then just counting dial settings, and the one trap is to forget that "working" is a position too. For a circuit with N lines: single stuck-at faults: each line can be s-a-0 or s-a-1, so there are 2N; multiple stuck-at faults: each line is in one of three states (fault-free, s-a-0, s-a-1), and at least one line must be faulty, so there are 3^N - 1; multiple faults with exactly k faulty lines: choose the k lines, then a stuck value for each: \binom{N}{k} 2^k. A circuit with N lines has exactly 2N single stuck-at faults and exactly 3^N - 1 multiple stuck-at faults (a single fault counts as a multiple fault with one faulty line). Moreover \sum_{k=1}^{N} \binom{N}{k} 2^k = 3^N - 1. Idea first: a multiple fault is a choice of state for every line, and each line has three states, not two. A fault (single or multiple) is completely described by saying, for every line, whether it is healthy, stuck at 0 or stuck at 1. Different descriptions give different faults, and every description in which at least one line is faulty is a fault. The number of descriptions is 3 \times 3 \times \dots \times 3 = 3^N (the product rule, one factor per line). Exactly one of them, "every line healthy", is the good circuit and not a fault. So there are 3^N - 1 multiple faults. Single faults are the descriptions with exactly one faulty line: N choices of the line times 2 stuck values, 2N. Grouping the 3^N - 1 descriptions by the number k of faulty lines: choose those lines in \binom{N}{k} ways and give each a stuck value in 2^k ways. Summing over k = 1, \dots, N counts every fault once, so \sum_{k \ge 1} \binom{N}{k} 2^k = 3^N - 1. This is also the binomial theorem: (1 + 2)^N = \sum_{k \ge 0} \binom{N}{k} 2^k, minus the k = 0 term. Sanity check. N = 1: a single line has two faults, and 3^1 - 1 = 2. N = 2: by listing, (0, –), (1, –), (–, 0), (–, 1), (0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1) is 8, and 3^2 - 1 = 8. Three wrong answers are waiting in every fault-countin

entries.title: Feedback, latches and races
headings: Worked examples: SR and NAND latches
Gated latches and the D latch
Worked examples: gated and D latches
Worked examples: rings, races and latch-or-flip-flop
entries.text:
Storage elements, lesson 1 of 3. Every circuit in Chapters 2 to 5 had a simple promise: tell me the inputs now and I will tell you the outputs now. Nothing that happened a second ago mattered. That promise is exactly what a computer cannot live with. A register must still hold a number after the wires that wrote it have moved on; a counter must know where it was to know where to go next. This chapter is about circuits that remember, and this first lesson finds the one ingredient that makes memory possible: feedback, a wire that carries a circuit's output back into its own input. We will learn to decide, for any loop, whether it settles, remembers or oscillates; build the classic one-bit memories, the SR latch from NOR gates and from NAND gates; meet the input pair that is "forbidden" and see, gate delay by gate delay, the race it causes; and tame the latch with an enable input, ending with the D latch and the multiplexer-with-feedback that GATE 2023 asked about. Where this fits Chapter 2, Lesson 6 taught you to evaluate a gate circuit line by line and to count its propagation delay. Every circuit there was acyclic: you could order the gates so that each one's inputs were already known. In Chapter 5, Lesson 1 we warned that a loop of gates breaks that rule and turns a circuit into a memory. This lesson is that warning taken seriously. The latches built here are the raw material of Lesson 2, where two of them are combined into an edge-triggered flip-flop, and of everything after it in this chapter: registers, counters and state machines are all flip-flops plus combinational logic. Feedback: how a circuit remembers A doorbell rings only while you press the button. Let go and it stops: the bell has no idea that anyone ever pressed it. That is a combinational circuit, output now = function of input now. A light switch is different. Flip it up and walk away: the light stays on. Flip it down and walk away: it stays off. The switch remembers the last thing you did to it, even though nobody is touching it now. How could gates, which only ever compute "output = function of inputs", behave like the switch? The trick is to let a gate see its own output. If an OR gate's output is wired back to one of its inputs, then once the output becomes 1, the gate is told "one of your inputs is 1", so it keeps saying 1, which keeps telling it that an input is 1, and so on, forever. The circuit is now holding itself up by its own bootstraps: the 1 is stored in the loop. Everything in this lesson is a careful version of that picture. A circuit has feedback when some gate's output can reach one of that same gate's inputs through a chain of wires and gates (the circuit graph has a cycle). The wire that closes the cycle is a feedback or loop wire, and its value is a state variable, written Q. A circuit with feedback is a sequential circuit: its output depends on its present inputs and on its past, because the past is stored in the loop. A circuit with no cycle is combinational: its outputs are a function of its present inputs alone (Chapter 5, Lesson 1 proves that). Notice what changes when we close a loop. In an acyclic circuit we can always compute the output: start from the inputs and work forward. In a loop there is no "forward": to compute Q we need Q. So the question "what is the output?" turns into a different question, "which values of Q are consistent with themselves?". Those consistent values are the circuit's possible resting states. Cut the feedback wire. On one side of the cut the circuit receives a value Q (the present state, "Q in"); on the other side it produces a value Q^+ (the next state, "Q out"). Because the rest of the circuit is acyclic, Q^+ is an ordinary Boolean function of the inputs x and of Q: Q^+ = f(x, Q), the loop function (also called the next-state or excitation function). A value Q is a stable state for input x when it reproduces itself: f(x, Q) = Q. When the circuit sits in a stable state and the input does not change, nothing in the circuit changes. When f(x, Q) 
eq Q, the loop wire is about to change, one propagation delay later; the state is unstable (transient). For a single loop wire there are only two candidate states, 0 and 1, and for a fixed input x the function f(x, \cdot) of one variable Q can only be one of four things: the constant 0, the constant 1, Q itself or \overline{Q}. Each gives a completely different kind of behaviour, and that is the whole classification. Let a circuit have one feedback wire Q with loop function f(x, Q), and fix the input x. If f(x, \cdot) is a constant c (0 or 1), the circuit has exactly one stable state, Q = c, and from either starting value it reaches it within one loop delay. The loop forgets: it acts like a combinational circuit with output c. If f(x, Q) = Q, both Q = 0 and Q = 1 are stable. The circuit keeps whichever value it had: it is a memory for this input. If f(x, Q) = \overline{Q}, no value is stable and the loop wire changes every loop delay: the circuit oscillates. In terms of the two values f(x, 0) and f(x, 1): Q = 0 is stable iff f(x, 0) = 0, and Q = 1 is stable iff f(x, 1) = 1. entries.text: Storage elements, lesson 2 of 3. Lesson 1 built a one-bit memory from two cross-coupled gates and then hit a wall: a latch is transparent while it is enabled, so if its output feeds back into its own input (as in every counter, register and state machine), the bit can change again and again during one enable pulse. This lesson builds the storage element that makes those loops safe, the flip-flop, which listens to its inputs only at one instant, the edge of a clock. We will build one from two latches (the master–slave pair), meet the four flip-flop types GATE uses (SR, JK, D and T) with their characteristic equations, see why a level-sensitive JK misbehaves (race-around), learn the excitation tables that run every design problem backwards, convert any flip-flop into any other, and finish with the timing rules (setup, hold, clock-to-Q, maximum clock frequency) and the method for reading the timing-diagram questions that GATE loves. Where this fits Lesson 1 ended with two promises: that a latch is a window and a flip-flop is a camera, and that a transparent latch cannot drive its own input without racing. This lesson keeps both promises. Lesson 3 analyses circuits with the characteristic equations of this lesson, Lesson 5 designs counters with its excitation tables, and registers (Lesson 6) and state machines (Lesson 7) rely on its timing rules. The one sentence to keep: a flip-flop's next state is computed from the inputs just before the active edge, and it appears just after it. Edge triggering: a camera, not a window Think of a photographer at a race. The runners move all the time, but the photo shows only where they were at the click. What happened a second before the click, or a second after, is not in the photo, and the photo does not change until the next click, however much the runners move. A flip-flop is that camera: the clock edge is the click, the inputs are the scene, and the output is the photo, held until the next click. A latch, in contrast, is a window: while it is open you see everything, as it happens. That is a disaster when the scene is you, as for a storage element whose output returns to its own input: you see your reflection change, react, see it change again. The camera breaks that loop, because the flip-flop's new output cannot get into the photo until the next click. A clock signal CLK has two kinds of edges: a rising (positive) edge, where it goes from 0 to 1, and a falling (negative) edge, where it goes from 1 to 0. A positive-edge-triggered flip-flop looks at its data inputs only at the rising edges of its clock. At each rising edge it computes its next state Q^+ from the inputs and the present state as they were just before the edge, and its output Q takes that value a short time after the edge (the clock-to-Q delay, defined later). Between edges, whatever the inputs do, Q does not change. A negative-edge-triggered flip-flop does the same at falling edges. Symbols: a small triangle (the dynamic indicator) on the clock pin marks an edge-triggered input; a bubble in front of the triangle means the falling edge is the active one. A plain clock pin with no triangle is a level-sensitive enable, which is a latch. Two phrases in the definition carry the whole lesson. "Just before the edge" tells you which value of the inputs counts: if an input changes at the edge, the value it had before the change is the one that is sampled (we will make this precise with the setup and hold times). "A short time after the edge" tells you when the output moves: never before the edge, and never in the middle of a clock period. Together they mean a flip-flop's output is a staircase that can only step at active edges. The animation drives a D latch and a positive-edge-triggered D flip-flop with the same clock and the same data waveform. Watch the clock's high phases: the latch output follows every wiggle of D while the clock is 1; the flip-flop output moves only at the rising edges, to the value D had just before each edge. Notice two things. When D changes in the middle of a high phase, the latch output changes and the flip-flop output does not. And a change of D that is undone before the next rising edge never reaches the flip-flop at all, a GATE trap we meet again at the end of the lesson. The most common error in a timing-diagram question is to let a flip-flop's output follow its input during the clock's high phase, as a latch would. If the clock pin has a triangle, the output can change only just after an active edge, and it takes the value of the input just before that edge. A student who lets Q follow D while CLK = 1 picks the option whose output rises in the middle of a clock pulse; examiners always include that option. The opposite error also happens: treating a gated latch (a clock ANDed with the inputs, no triangle) as edge-triggered and ignoring a change in the middle of the enable pulse, which a latch does pass through. A flip-flop samples its inputs at an active edge (rising or falling) and changes its output only just after that edge; between edges it ignores its inputs. A latch is transparent for the whole time its enable is active. Read inputs just before the edge; move outputs just after it. Building an edge from two latches: master–slave An airlock on a spaceship has two doors, and the rule is that they are never open at the same time. To go out, you open the inner door, step in, close it, and only then open the outer door. At no moment is there an open path from the inside of the ship to space. Two latches can be arranged the same way. The first latch, the master, is open while the clock is 1; the second, the slave, is open while the clock is 0. While the clock is 1 the master follows the input, but the slave is closed, so nothing reaches the output. When the clock falls, the master closes (keeping whatever it had at that instant) and the slave opens, copying the master to the output. entries.text: Storage elements, lesson 3 of 3. Lesson 2 gave us four flip-flops and their characteristic equations, one flip-flop at a time. Real circuits wire several flip-flops together, feed each one's output into the logic that drives the others, and let a single clock tick them all at once. GATE then hands you such a circuit and asks what it does: which state comes next, what the flip-flops hold after four clocks, which states can never appear, what bit sequence comes out. This lesson teaches one method that answers every one of those questions. We will see why synchronous circuits (one clock for every flip-flop) are the ones we can analyse at all, turn a circuit into input equations, state equations and a state table, draw the state diagram, trace it clock by clock without the classic update-order mistake, find the states that are reachable and the cycle every circuit must fall into, and read outputs at the right moment. Thirteen GATE questions, from 1991 to 2023, are all instances of this one procedure. Where this fits Lesson 1 showed what feedback does inside a single storage cell, and Lesson 2 built the edge-triggered flip-flop whose output moves only just after a clock edge. This lesson zooms out from one flip-flop to a machine of several. The tools are the ones you already have: the characteristic equations Q^+ = D, Q^+ = T \oplus Q and Q^+ = J\overline{Q} + \overline{K}Q from Lesson 2, and the plain combinational evaluation of Chapter 2 for the gates between the flip-flops. What is new is the bookkeeping: how to organise the work so that the answer to any question can be read off one table. The same table is the starting point of counter design in Lesson 5, of registers in Lesson 6 and of state machines in Lesson 7, where we run the procedure backwards. What a synchronous sequential circuit is Think of a board game. Your position on the board right now and the number on the dice decide where you will be after your turn, and the rule that turns "position and dice" into "next position" is printed in the rule book. Between turns nothing moves. The game is completely described by the rule book: if you know where you are and what you roll, you know where you will be. A synchronous sequential circuit is that game played by wires. The position is the set of bits held in the flip-flops (the state), the dice are the external inputs, the turn is a clock edge, and the rule book is the gate logic wired in front of the flip-flops. Analysing a circuit means writing its rule book down in a form you can read: a table with one row per position and roll. Once that table exists, every question about the game ("where am I after four turns?", "can I ever land on square 5?") is answered by reading it. A sequential circuit is combinational logic plus memory, with feedback: some outputs of the logic are stored and come back as inputs. In a synchronous (clocked) sequential circuit, the memory is a set of edge-triggered flip-flops that all receive the same clock. The state can change only at the active clock edges, and at each edge every flip-flop loads the value its input logic produced from the state and inputs before the edge. Between edges the state is constant. In an asynchronous sequential circuit there is no common clock. The memory is the delay of the feedback loops themselves (or unclocked latches), and the state changes whenever an input change works its way round a loop. The state of a synchronous circuit with n flip-flops is an n-bit word, so it has at most 2^n states. Its behaviour is fixed by two functions of the present state and the inputs: the next-state function (what the flip-flops will hold after the edge) and the output function. Why does the clock make such a difference? In an asynchronous circuit two state bits that must change together never change at exactly the same instant: one gate is a little faster, and for a moment the circuit is in a third state that nobody planned (a race, the subject of Lesson 1). A combinational path with a hazard can produce a brief glitch, and a loop can latch onto that glitch. In a synchronous circuit both problems are still there physically, but they happen between edges, while the flip-flops are not listening. The theorem below makes that precise; it is the single reason the whole industry designs synchronously. Let a synchronous circuit have flip-flops with clock-to-Q delay at most t_{cq} and setup time t_{su}, combinational next-state logic whose longest path is t_{logic,max}, external inputs that change only just after edges, and hold times met. If the clock period satisfies T \ge t_{cq} + t_{logic,max} + t_{su}, then at every active edge each flip-flop samples the settled value of its input logic, computed from the state held during the previous clock period. Consequently, glitches, hazards and races inside the combinational logic cannot change the stored state, and the circuit behaves exactly as its state table says. Idea first: after an edge, everything that can move settles within t_{cq} + t_{logic,max}; the next edge looks only during its setup window, which starts after that settling time. Take an edge at time 0. Every flip-flop output changes (if at all) by time t_{cq}, and the external inputs change just after the edge too. From then on, the inputs of the combinational logic are constant until the next edge. A combinational circuit with constant inputs can glitch (a hazard), but after its longest path delay its outputs are the correct Boolean function of those inputs and stay there. So by time t_{cq} + t_{logic,max} every flip-flop input holds its final value, the next-state function evaluated on the present state and inputs. The next edge comes at time T. A flip-flop needs its input stable from T - t_{su} to the edge (Lesson 2's sampling window). The assumption T \ge t_{cq} + t_{logic,max} + t_{su} is the same as T - t_{su} \ge t_{cq} + t_{logic,max}: the window opens only after the logic has settled. entries.text: Counters and registers, lesson 1 of 3. A counter is the simplest useful sequential circuit: a handful of flip-flops that step through a fixed list of states, one step per clock pulse. Counters measure time, divide clock frequencies, generate addresses and sequence the steps of every controller. This lesson starts with the vocabulary every counter question uses (modulus, up and down, synchronous and asynchronous), the one formula GATE asks most often (how many flip-flops a mod-N counter needs), and the arithmetic of counting pulses with wrap-around. Then it builds the cheapest counter of all, the ripple counter, in which each flip-flop clocks the next, and studies its three faces: as a counter (up or down, depending on one wiring choice), as a frequency divider (each stage halves the frequency), and as a slow, glitchy circuit (the carry ripples through the stages one delay at a time). It ends with the standard trick for a counter of any modulus, the asynchronous clear. Where this fits Lesson 2 gave us the T flip-flop, whose next state is T \oplus Q: with T = 1 it toggles at every active edge. That single fact is the whole engine of this lesson. Lesson 3 analysed synchronous circuits, in which every flip-flop shares one clock; a ripple counter breaks that rule on purpose, and we will see what it buys and what it costs. Lesson 5 then designs synchronous counters for any sequence, and Lesson 6 builds counters from shift registers (ring and Johnson counters). The sentence to keep: in a ripple counter, stage i toggles when stage i - 1 makes the transition that carries (or borrows), and every stage adds one propagation delay. What a counter is Look at the mileage counter of an old car. It is a row of wheels, each printed with the digits 0 to 9. The rightmost wheel turns once per tenth of a kilometre. Every time it rolls over from 9 to 0, it nudges the wheel to its left forward by one digit; when that wheel rolls over, it nudges the next one, and so on. Nobody drives the left wheels directly: each wheel is driven by the roll-over of its right-hand neighbour. A binary counter is the same machine with two-digit wheels (0 and 1). The rightmost bit flips at every clock pulse; whenever a bit rolls over from 1 back to 0, it pushes the next bit forward. Notice that the odometer already contains both ideas of this lesson: the count (the digits shown) and the ripple (a roll-over at 0999 → 1000 travels from the right wheel to the left one, wheel by wheel, and for a moment the display shows numbers that are neither 0999 nor 1000). A counter is a sequential circuit that steps through a fixed cyclic sequence of states, one step for each active edge of its input (the clock or the pulses being counted). The modulus (mod) of a counter is the number of distinct states in its cycle. A mod-N counter returns to its starting state after every N pulses. An n-bit binary counter that uses all its states is mod-2^n; one that skips some states (for example a decade counter, 0 to 9) has a modulus below 2^n. An up counter steps through 0, 1, 2, \dots, N - 1, 0, \dots; a down counter through N - 1, N - 2, \dots, 1, 0, N - 1, \dots (from 0 the next state of a down counter is the largest state). An up/down counter has a mode input that chooses the direction. In a synchronous counter every flip-flop is clocked by the same clock signal, and gates in front of the flip-flop inputs decide which bits change (Lesson 5). In an asynchronous (or ripple) counter only the first flip-flop receives the clock; each later flip-flop is clocked by an output of the flip-flop before it. The state of an n-bit counter is written Q_{n-1} \dots Q_1 Q_0, with Q_0 the least significant bit (the one that changes at every pulse in a binary counter). A counter is therefore "a register plus a rule". Two numbers describe it from the outside, the modulus and the direction, and one fact describes it from the inside, how its flip-flops are clocked. GATE asks about all three, and the first question is always the cheapest one: how many flip-flops? A mod-N counter (N \ge 2) built with binary-coded states needs at least k = \lceil \log_2 N \rceil flip-flops, and that many are enough. Equivalently, k is the smallest integer with 2^k \ge N. With other state codes the count changes: a one-hot code (one flip-flop per state, exactly one of them 1) uses N flip-flops, and a Johnson (twisted-ring) code uses N/2 flip-flops for an even N. Idea first: a counter must remember how many pulses it has seen (modulo N), and k bits can remember at most 2^k different things. At least \lceil \log_2 N \rceil. After 0, 1, \dots, N - 1 pulses (from the starting state) a mod-N counter is in N different states, because a mod-N counter first returns to its start after exactly N pulses: if the states after i and j pulses (0 \le i < j < N) were equal, the counter would repeat with period j - i < N, and its cycle would have fewer than N states. The state lives in k flip-flops, which can hold only 2^k different bit patterns. So 2^k \ge N, which means k \ge \log_2 N, and since k is an integer, k \ge \lceil \log_2 N \rceil. Enough. With k = \lceil \log_2 N \rceil we have 2^k \ge N, so the patterns for 0, 1, \dots, N - 1 exist; a binary counter that counts up and returns to 0 after N - 1 realises the cycle (we build one with an asynchronous clear at the end of this lesson, and one with no clear in Lesson 5). Other codes. One-hot uses one flip-flop per state by definition: N. A Johnson counter of m flip-flops cycles through 2m states, so a mod-N Johnson counter needs m = N/2. ∎ Sanity check. N = 2^k exactly: \lceil \log_2 2^k \rceil = k, and k bits have exactly 2^k patterns, all used. One more state, N = 2^k + 1, already needs k + 1 flip-flops. seqlib.ff_count returns 4 for mod-10, 8 for mod-256 and 9 for mod-257 and mod-258. entries.text: Counters and registers, lesson 2 of 3. Lesson 4 built counters in which each flip-flop clocks the next. They are cheap, but they are slow, they show false states, and they can only count in binary. This lesson builds the other kind: synchronous counters, in which one clock drives every flip-flop and a little combinational logic in front of the flip-flops decides which bits change. That one change of wiring buys two things. The counter becomes fast (every bit settles one flip-flop delay after the edge, whatever the width), and it becomes programmable: by choosing the logic we can make the flip-flops step through any sequence we like, a Gray code, a jumbled order such as 1, 4, 2, 3, a counter that saturates at its top value, or a counter that goes up or down on command. We will learn the one design procedure that produces all of them (state table, excitation columns, K-maps, equations), see why D, T and JK flip-flops give different but equally correct circuits, and then meet the two places where students and even textbooks go wrong: sequences that repeat values (the state is not the output) and unused states that can trap the counter for ever (lock-out). Ten GATE questions from 1991 to 2026 test exactly these ideas. Where this fits Lesson 2 gave us the excitation tables: for each flip-flop type, the inputs that take it from Q to a wanted Q^+. Lesson 3 taught us to go from a circuit to its state table. Design is the same road travelled the other way: from a wanted state table back to a circuit. The middle of that road is pure combinational minimisation, the K-maps and prime implicants of Chapter 3 (prime implicants and don't-cares), so everything you know about grouping 1s and using don't-cares comes back here, with one new danger: in a counter, a don't-care is not harmless, because it decides where the circuit goes if it ever lands in an unused state. Lesson 6 builds counters out of shift registers, and Lesson 7 generalises this lesson's procedure from counters (no input, or a mode input) to state machines with inputs and outputs. The sentence to keep: list the next state of every state, read off what each flip-flop must do, minimise, and then check every state of the circuit you built, including the ones you never wanted. The synchronous binary counter A ripple counter is an odometer whose wheels push each other: the right wheel rolls over and physically kicks the next one. Imagine instead an odometer whose wheels never touch. Every wheel has its own little motor, and all the motors are switched by one shared button. Before each press, a clerk looks at the whole display and writes a note for every wheel: "you turn this time", or "you stay". Then the button is pressed and every wheel obeys its note at the same instant. That clerk is the combinational logic of a synchronous counter, and the notes are the flip-flop inputs. Designing the counter means writing the clerk's rule book: for every possible display, say which way each wheel must move. For plain binary counting the rule book is short and famous; for any other sequence we will learn to write it systematically. What is the rule for binary counting? Adding 1 flips the lowest bit always; it flips bit 1 when bit 0 was 1 (a carry comes in); it flips bit 2 when bits 0 and 1 were both 1; and so on. "Flip or stay" is exactly what a T flip-flop understands (Q^+ = T \oplus Q), so a T flip-flop per bit plus a few AND gates is the natural binary counter. An n-bit synchronous binary up counter has n T flip-flops (or JK flip-flops with J = K) on one common clock, with T_0 = 1, \qquad T_i = Q_0\,Q_1 \cdots Q_{i-1}\quad (i \ge 1). For three bits: T_0 = 1, T_1 = Q_0, T_2 = Q_1 Q_0; a fourth bit adds T_3 = Q_2 Q_1 Q_0. The AND terms can be built in two ways: parallel (look-ahead) gating: one AND gate per stage, with i inputs for stage i, so every T_i is one gate delay after the flip-flop outputs settle; ripple-carry (serial) gating: a chain in which each AND takes the previous AND's output and one more Q (T_{i+1} = T_i \cdot Q_i), so every gate has only two inputs, but the signal for stage i passes through a chain of gates. All flip-flops change together, one clock-to-output delay t_{cq} after the active edge: there is no carry rippling through the flip-flops, only (in the serial version) through the gates, and that settles before the next edge. When an n-bit binary number Q_{n-1}\dots Q_1Q_0 is incremented (modulo 2^n), bit i changes if and only if Q_0 = Q_1 = \dots = Q_{i-1} = 1; bit 0 always changes. Hence the T inputs T_0 = 1 and T_i = Q_0 Q_1 \cdots Q_{i-1} make a synchronous binary up counter, and a down counter uses T_i = \overline{Q_0}\,\overline{Q_1} \cdots \overline{Q_{i-1}}. Idea first: adding 1 is column addition with a carry; a column changes exactly when a carry arrives, and a carry arrives exactly when every column to its right was 1. Add 1 in the lowest column. Column 0 receives the 1 and always changes. Column j passes a carry to column j + 1 exactly when column j received a carry and held 1 (since 1 + 1 = 10); if it held 0, it absorbs the carry and the addition stops there. By induction on i, column i receives a carry exactly when columns 0, \dots, i - 1 all held 1, and a column changes exactly when it receives a carry. So bit i toggles iff Q_0 \cdots Q_{i-1} = 1, which is T_i = Q_0 \cdots Q_{i-1} in the characteristic equation Q_i^+ = T_i \oplus Q_i. The wrap from 11\dots1 to 00\dots0 is the case where every column toggles. For subtraction a borrow passes through a column that held 0, which gives T_i = \overline{Q_0} \cdots \overline{Q_{i-1}}. ∎ Check by design. entries.text: Counters and registers, lesson 3 of 3. A register is a row of flip-flops that holds a word. A shift register is a register whose flip-flops are wired in a chain, so that at every clock edge each bit moves one place along. That one idea does a surprising amount of work: it turns a serial stream of bits into a parallel word and back again, it delays a signal by an exact number of clocks, and, once the end of the chain is fed back to its beginning, it becomes a counter. This lesson builds the shift register from D flip-flops, counts exactly how many clocks it takes to load and to empty one (a count that is easy to get wrong), adds parallel load and the four-mode universal register, and shows how a RAM with a counter can pretend to be a 1024-stage shift register. Then it closes the loop three ways: the ring counter (the last output fed straight back), the Johnson counter (the last output fed back inverted) and the linear feedback shift register, or LFSR (an XOR of some stages fed back), and studies the state cycles each one makes, including the cycles nobody wanted. Where this fits Lesson 2 gave us the D flip-flop, which simply copies D to Q at the clock edge. Lesson 3 taught the analysis procedure: next-state equations, state table, a trace from the given start, and the cycles every autonomous circuit falls into. In a shift register every next-state equation is just "copy your neighbour", so this lesson uses that procedure constantly without spelling it out. Lesson 4 named the three ways to code a counter's states (binary, one-hot and Johnson) and promised that the last two are shift registers; here they are. The sentence to keep: in a shift register every stage copies the stage before it on the same clock edge, so the only freedom left is what you feed into the first stage. The shift register Picture a line of people passing buckets of water from a well to a fire. Each person holds one bucket. When the whistle blows, everybody hands their bucket to the person on their right at the same moment, and the first person takes a new bucket from the well. The last person's bucket goes onto the fire. Three things about the brigade are worth noticing before we build it. First, everybody moves together, on the whistle: nobody passes a bucket early, and nobody takes one twice. Second, a bucket that enters at the well needs one whistle per person to reach the fire, so the line is a delay. Third, at any moment you can walk along the line and look into every bucket at once (that is "parallel out"), or stand at the end and watch them arrive one at a time ("serial out"). A shift register is this brigade with D flip-flops as the people and the clock edge as the whistle. An n-bit shift register is a chain of n edge-triggered D flip-flops Q_1, Q_2, \dots, Q_n on one common clock, wired so that each stage copies the one before it: D_1 = SI \ (\text{the serial input}), \qquad D_i = Q_{i-1} \quad (i = 2, \dots, n). The serial output is SO = Q_n, the end of the chain; the parallel outputs are all of Q_1 \dots Q_n. We write the contents left to right as Q_1Q_2\dots Q_n, with the serial input entering on the left, so at every active edge the word moves one place to the right: the new bit lands in Q_1, every bit moves one stage on, and the old Q_n falls off the end. Because every flip-flop samples its input at the same edge, each one takes the value its neighbour had before the edge (the synchronous discipline of Lesson 3). That is why the chain moves the word exactly one place per clock and never "races" a bit through several stages at once. As state equations: Q_1^+ = SI, Q_2^+ = Q_1, …, Q_n^+ = Q_{n-1}. Every number in this lesson comes from iterating those equations (or a version with something more interesting in place of SI). Notice what they do not contain: there is no gate between the stages, so a shift register is as fast as a single flip-flop, whatever n is. One small point before we count clocks. The two ends of the chain are often drawn the other way round (the input on the right, shifting left), and GATE questions use both. Nothing in the theory changes, but every trace must start by asking where the bits enter and which bit enters first. We come back to this in a trap. Feed an n-stage shift register, starting from any contents, with a serial stream b_1, b_2, b_3, \dots, where b_k is the value at SI when edge k arrives. Then after edge k the stage Q_i holds b_{k-i+1} (for k \ge i). In particular the serial output after edge k is SO = Q_n = b_{k-n+1}, so each bit appears at the output n - 1 edges after the edge that took it in, and is present there during the n-th clock period after the one in which it was applied. For an n-bit word b_1 \dots b_n entered into a register that holds older data: the first bit reaches the output after edge n; the last bit reaches the output after edge 2n - 1, so all n bits have been seen at the output after 2n - 1 clocks; after edge 2n the last bit has been shifted out, and none of the word is left in the register. Idea first: each edge moves every bit exactly one stage, so a bit's stage number is "edges since it entered, plus one". Induction on k. After edge k, Q_1 = b_k, because D_1 = SI and SI = b_k at that edge. For i \ge 2, Q_i^+ = Q_{i-1}, so the value of Q_i after edge k is the value of Q_{i-1} after edge k - 1, which by the induction hypothesis is b_{(k-1)-(i-1)+1} = b_{k-i+1}. That proves the formula for every stage, and i = n gives SO = b_{k-n+1}. The three counts. Bit b_1 is at the output when k - n + 1 = 1, i.e. after edge n. Bit b_n is at the output when k - n + 1 = n, i.e. after edge 2n - 1. At edge 2n the output stage takes b_{n+1}, a bit that is not part of the word, and every other stage holds a later bit still; so after 2n edges the word has left. ∎ Check by simulation. seqlib.shift_right run on a cleared 4-bit register with the word 1, 1, 0, 1 followed by zeros puts the first bit at Q_4 after clock 4, the last after clock 7, and leaves 0000 after clock 8.

entries.title: Finite state machines: Mealy and Moore
headings: From words to a state diagram
Worked examples: from words to a diagram
From a state machine to a circuit
Worked examples: from machine to hardware
entries.text: State machines, lesson 1 of 2. Every circuit in this chapter so far has been a state machine in disguise. A latch remembers one bit, a counter walks round a cycle, a shift register remembers the last few inputs. This lesson takes off the disguise. A finite state machine (FSM) is a synchronous circuit described not by its gates but by its behaviour: a finite set of states (what it must remember), an input that arrives once per clock, a rule that gives the next state, and a rule that gives the output. There are exactly two ways to attach the output: to the state alone (a Moore machine) or to the state and the present input together (a Mealy machine), and the difference decides when the output appears, the first thing a designer must get right. We will learn to turn a sentence of English into a state diagram, to build the most famous kind of FSM, the sequence detector, to read off what a given machine computes (a 2's complementer, an adder of consecutive bits, a run editor), to find the shortest input that drives a machine to a target, and finally to turn a state diagram into flip-flops and gates, choosing the state codes (binary, Gray or one-hot) along the way. Six GATE questions from 2001 to 2021 test these skills. Where this fits Lesson 3 went from a circuit to its state table; Lesson 5 went back from a wanted state table to a circuit, for counters, whose only input (if any) was a mode or an enable. A state machine is the general case of both: the table has an input column that matters in every row, and an output that is not just the state bits. Everything you learned there still applies: the excitation tables of Lesson 2, K-maps with don't-cares from Chapter 3, the rule that every flip-flop is updated from the old state, and the lock-out warning for unused states. The next lesson, State minimisation, asks how few states a machine can have. The mathematics of finite automata, regular languages and DFA/NFA constructions belongs to the Theory of Computation subject; here we use machines the way a hardware designer does: to specify, time and build circuits. The sentence to keep: decide what the machine must remember, give each memory a state, give every state an arc for every input, and then decide whether the output belongs to the state (Moore) or to the arc (Mealy). Mealy and Moore machines A vending machine sells a drink for 15 rupees and accepts 5- and 10-rupee coins. It cannot see your wallet or your history; all it can do is remember how much has been paid so far: 0, 5 or 10 (at 15 or more it vends and starts again). Those three amounts are its states. A coin is an input. The machine's whole behaviour is a small table: "in state 5, a 10-rupee coin makes me vend and go back to 0". Nothing else about the past matters, because the amount paid is all the machine needs to decide what to do next. That is the idea of a finite state machine. Its state is a summary of the past, just detailed enough to decide the future. Now ask: when does the drink fall? One design drops it the moment the last coin lands (the output depends on the state and the coin: Mealy). Another first moves to a "vend" state and drops the drink while it is in that state (the output depends on the state alone: Moore). Both sell drinks correctly; they differ in timing and in the number of states. That difference is the first thing to master. A finite state machine has a finite set of states S with a start state s_0, an input alphabet X (for us usually \{0, 1\}), an output alphabet Z, and a next-state function \delta(s, x) that gives the state after the clock edge when the present state is s and the present input is x. The output is given in one of two ways. Moore machine: the output is a function of the present state only, z = \lambda(s). In a state diagram the output is written inside the state circle ("S3/1"), and arcs carry only the input. Mealy machine: the output is a function of the present state and the present input, z = \lambda(s, x). In a state diagram the output is written on the arc, as "input/output" (an arc "1/0" means: on input 1, output 0 and follow this arc). In hardware both are a register of flip-flops holding the state plus two blocks of combinational logic: the next-state logic (from s and x to the flip-flop inputs) and the output logic. In a Moore machine the output logic sees only the flip-flop outputs; in a Mealy machine it also sees the input wires directly. Every machine in this chapter is synchronous: the state changes only at the active clock edge, and the input is sampled just before that edge. A state table lists, for every present state and every input, the next state and the output. Two layouts are common: Compact: one row per present state, one next-state column per input value and (Mealy) one output column per input value, or (Moore) a single output column. Entries such as "B/0" in an "x = 1" column mean "next state B, output 0". Long: one row per (present state, input) pair, with the state written in bits: present-state bits, input, next-state bits, output. GATE 2009 used this layout with the present-state bits A, B first, then the input, then the next-state bits, then the output. The table and the diagram carry the same information: each row of the long table is one arc. A table is complete when every state has a next state for every input; an arc that is missing must either never happen (a don't-care, as in Lesson 3) or be a mistake. Read the column headings before the numbers: in a long table, mixing up which columns are the present state and which are the next state reverses every arc. The two kinds of machine are not rivals: each can imitate the other, at a price. Every Moore machine M has a Mealy machine M' with the same states whose output on input x in state s is \lambda'(s, x) = \lambda(\delta(s, x)): it produces, during the period of each input, the output M produces in the period after it (one clock earlier than M). entries.text: State machines, lesson 2 of 2. Lesson 7 turned word problems into state tables and state tables into flip-flops and gates. It did not ask whether the table had too many states. Tables written by hand often do: two states that were invented for different reasons ("I have just seen a 0", "I have just been reset") may turn out to behave identically for every input that could ever follow. Such states are equivalent, and a machine that keeps both of them pays for a state it does not need: possibly an extra flip-flop, and certainly extra rows in every K-map. This lesson makes "behave identically" precise, proves the two standard procedures that find all equivalent states (partition refinement and the implication table), shows how to count the states a word specification needs without drawing a table at all, and ends with what minimisation buys in hardware and what it does not. Where this fits Lesson 7 gave us Mealy and Moore machines, their state tables and state diagrams, and the procedure from a table to a circuit: assign codes, write the excitation table, minimise the input equations. Minimising the number of states comes before state assignment: fewer states means fewer codes to assign, often fewer flip-flops (an n-state machine needs \lceil \log_2 n \rceil of them, as in Lesson 4), and more unused codes that become don't-cares in the K-maps of Lesson 5. The same refinement algorithm minimises DFAs. The language-theoretic side (Myhill–Nerode, uniqueness of the minimal DFA, regular languages) belongs to the Theory of Computation subject and is not re-taught here. We prove the algorithm only for Mealy and Moore output machines, as GATE asks it on state tables. The sentence to keep: two states are equivalent when no input sequence can ever tell them apart by the outputs, and a minimal machine keeps one state per class of equivalent states. Equivalent states and k-equivalence A shop has two assistants at the counter. You cannot see them; you can only hand in questions one after another and read the answers. Suppose that, whatever sequence of questions you hand in, the answers that come back are exactly the same whether assistant P or assistant Q is on duty. Then, as far as any customer can ever tell, P and Q are interchangeable: the shop can send one of them home and nobody will notice. Notice what we did not require. P and Q may think differently, use different notebooks, and walk to different shelves; all that matters is that the answers agree for every possible sequence of questions. Notice also how strong "every" is: agreeing on the first question, or on the first ten, is not enough. A single question sequence, however long, that makes them answer differently means they are not interchangeable. A state of a sequential machine is an assistant. The input sequence is the list of questions, and the output sequence is the list of answers. Two states that can never be told apart by the outputs are redundant copies of one another, and the machine needs only one of them. Let M be a completely specified machine with next-state function \delta(p, x) and output \lambda(p, x) (Mealy) or \lambda(p) (Moore). For an input string w = x_1x_2\dots x_k, write \lambda(p, w) for the output sequence that M produces when it starts in state p and reads w (for a Moore machine, the outputs of the states visited, including \lambda(p) itself). Two states p and q are equivalent, written p \equiv q, when \lambda(p, w) = \lambda(q, w) \quad \text{for every input string } w. They are distinguishable when some string w gives different output sequences; such a w is a distinguishing string for the pair. A machine is minimal (reduced) when no two of its states are equivalent. The definition talks about infinitely many strings, so it cannot be checked by trying them all. The rest of the lesson turns it into a finite procedure. The first step is to see that equivalence behaves like equality, so the states fall into clean classes. For any completely specified machine: \equiv is reflexive (p \equiv p), symmetric (p \equiv q \Rightarrow q \equiv p) and transitive (p \equiv q and q \equiv r \Rightarrow p \equiv r), so the states split into disjoint equivalence classes. Closure: if p \equiv q then for every input x the outputs agree, \lambda(p, x) = \lambda(q, x) (Mealy) or \lambda(p) = \lambda(q) (Moore), and the next states are equivalent: \delta(p, x) \equiv \delta(q, x). Merging: build M' with one state [p] per class, \delta'([p], x) = [\delta(p, x)] and \lambda'([p], x) = \lambda(p, x) (Moore: \lambda'([p]) = \lambda(p)). This is well defined (it does not depend on which member p we pick), and M' started in [p] produces the same output sequence as M started in p, for every string. Idea first: "has the same output sequence for every string" is equality of two infinite tables of outputs, and equality is always reflexive, symmetric and transitive. Closure says that a common future stays common after one step, and merging uses closure to show that the merged machine can never notice which member it is standing in. Part 1. \lambda(p, w) = \lambda(p, w) for every w, so p \equiv p. If \lambda(p, w) = \lambda(q, w) for every w, then \lambda(q, w) = \lambda(p, w) for every w. If \lambda(p, w) = \lambda(q, w) and \lambda(q, w) = \lambda(r, w) for every w, then \lambda(p, w) = \lambda(r, w) for every w. A relation with these three properties splits a set into disjoint classes. Part 2. Take the one-symbol string w = x: the outputs must agree. Now take any string v. The output sequence of xv from p is the outputs read before and during the first input (\lambda(p, x) for Mealy, \lambda(p) for Moore) followed by the output sequence of v from \delta(p, x), and the same for q. Since \lambda(p, xv) = \lambda(q, xv) and the first parts agree, the remaining parts agree: \lambda(\delta(p, x), v) = \lambda(\delta(q, x), v) for every v, which is \delta(p, x) \equiv \delta(q, x). headings: Memory vocabulary: words, addresses and kinds of memory
Inside a chip: the cell array and its decoders
Worked examples: chips, arrays and cells
Address maps: which chip answers which address
entries.text: Optional: beyond the core GATE syllabus. The current GATE CSE syllabus lists no memory chips under Digital Logic, and no Digital Logic question in our bank asks about them. We still teach this lesson for one practical reason: every memory question in Computer Organisation uses exactly this arithmetic. How many address lines does a chip need? How many chips make a bigger memory, and how are they wired? Which chip answers address 9A3C? Why does main memory need refreshing while a cache does not? These are questions about how a memory is organised, and the answers are short once you see a memory as a grid of cells, a decoder that picks one row, and a few rules for stacking chips. This lesson builds those rules from scratch, proves the two counting facts you will use most, and works fourteen examples, four of them edge cases that cost marks in COA papers. Where this fits Chapter 5, Lesson 5 treated a ROM as a truth table wired in silicon: an address decoder feeding an OR array. It also showed how to build a bigger ROM from small chips. Here we widen the view to every kind of semiconductor memory, writable ones included, look inside the chip (cell array, row and column decoders), and make the expansion recipe precise for both directions (wider words, more words). The decoders themselves come from Chapter 5, Lesson 3, whose section on address decoding for memory introduced the chip-select decoder; the static RAM cell is the latch of Chapter 6, Lesson 1. The tri-state ("floating") outputs that let many chips share one data bus reappear at transistor level in Lesson 3. Memory hierarchies, caches and interleaving belong to the Computer Organisation subject; we stop at the chip and the board. Memory vocabulary: words, addresses and kinds of memory Picture a library with a long row of shelves. Every shelf has a number painted on it, and every shelf holds the same number of book slots. To fetch something you never search: you say a shelf number, a librarian walks straight to that shelf, and hands you everything on it, all slots at once. A memory chip is that library. A shelf is a word, its number is the address, and the slots on a shelf are the bits of the word. You never ask for "bit 37 of the whole memory"; you ask for "word 5" and get all of its bits together. Two questions about any memory therefore have two separate answers: how many shelves (that decides how long the shelf numbers must be, the address lines) and how wide is each shelf (that decides how many bits come out at once, the data lines). Mixing those two numbers up is the most common memory mistake there is. A memory stores W words of B bits each; we write its organisation as W \times B ("W by B") and its capacity as W \cdot B bits. Each word has an address from 0 to W - 1, carried on k address lines, and a word enters or leaves on B data lines. Sizes use binary prefixes: 1\text{K} = 2^{10} = 1024, 1\text{M} = 2^{20}, 1\text{G} = 2^{30}. A 4\text{K} \times 8 chip holds 4096 words of 8 bits, so 32\,768 bits = 32 Kbit = 4 KB. Besides address and data lines a chip has control inputs: chip select \overline{CS} (or enable), which must be active for the chip to respond at all, write enable \overline{WE} (or a single R/\overline{W} line) and often output enable \overline{OE}. A deselected chip puts its data outputs in the high-impedance state: it neither drives 0 nor 1, so many chips can share one data bus and only the selected one speaks. Random access means that the time to reach a word does not depend on its address (unlike a tape or a shift register). The memories are grouped by what happens to the data: Memory that loses its contents when power is removed is volatile (SRAM and DRAM); the ROM family is non-volatile. "RAM" in everyday use means the read-write, volatile kind, although a ROM is just as randomly accessible. How many digits must the shelf numbers have? With 2-digit decimal numbers you can label 100 shelves; with 3 digits, 1000. A memory labels its words in binary, so k address lines can name 2^k words. To label W words you need the smallest k with 2^k \ge W. Notice what does not appear in that sentence: the width of the shelf. A shelf holding 1 book and a shelf holding 64 books need the same shelf number. A memory of W words needs exactly k = \lceil \log_2 W \rceil address lines, whatever its word width B. For W = 2^k (every real chip) this is k = \log_2 W, and every one of the 2^k addresses names a word. Idea first: k wires carry 2^k different patterns, and each word needs its own pattern. With k address lines there are exactly 2^k distinct address patterns. If 2^k < W, two of the W words would have to share a pattern (pigeonhole), and the memory could not tell them apart, so 2^k \ge W is necessary. Conversely, with k = \lceil \log_2 W \rceil we have 2^k \ge W, and numbering the words 0, 1, \dots, W - 1 in binary gives each its own pattern, so k lines suffice. The width B never entered the argument: all B bits of a word share that word's address. A 32\text{K} \times 8 chip holds 256 Kbit. The tempting wrong answer for its address lines is \log_2(256\text{K}) = 18, which counts bits. The memory addresses words: \log_2(32\text{K}) = 15 address lines and 8 data lines. The opposite slip, using bytes when the memory is word-addressable, gives the same kind of error: 4 KB of 32-bit words is 1024 words, so 10 address lines, not 12. Inside a chip: the cell array and its decoders If you built a 1\text{M} \times 1 memory literally as a list, its address decoder would need a million output wires, one per word, each running the full width of the chip. Nobody builds that. Instead the million cells are folded into a square, 1024 rows by 1024 columns. Half of the address bits pick a row (a 10-to-1024 decoder drives the word lines), and the other half pick a column inside that row (a 10-to-1024 column decoder, or a multiplexer, selects one bit line).
