entries.title: DAC and ADC basics
headings: Worked examples: ADC codes and conversion times
Successive approximation: a binary search in hardware
entries.text: Optional: beyond the core GATE syllabus. Every circuit in this subject so far lives in a world of two voltages, "low" and "high", 0 and 1. The world outside does not: a microphone, a thermometer or a battery produces a voltage that can take any value in a range. Two circuits sit on the border. A digital-to-analog converter (DAC) takes an n-bit number and produces a voltage proportional to it; an analog-to-digital converter (ADC) does the reverse, measuring a voltage and writing it down as an n-bit number. This lesson builds both from parts you already know: resistors that turn binary weights into currents, comparators that answer one yes/no question each, and a register that plays a binary search. We prove the two facts that make the classic circuits work (the R-2R ladder halves its current at every node; successive approximation finds the right code in exactly n steps), and we count what each ADC design costs in comparators and in clock cycles. Where this fits The number a DAC reads is a binary fraction in disguise: the code b_{n-1}\dots b_0 is turned into the voltage V_{ref} \times 0.b_{n-1}\dots b_0, which is the fixed-point reading of Chapter 1, Lesson 3. The flash ADC ends in a priority encoder, the circuit of Chapter 5, Lesson 3, and the successive-approximation ADC is a register driven by a small sequential controller (the registers of Chapter 6, Lesson 6 and the state machines of Lesson 7). The other two lessons of this optional chapter are memory organisation and logic families. Analog details (operational amplifiers, settling time, noise) belong to an electronics course; here we keep to what the digital side has to know: the arithmetic of the codes. Two converters, one staircase Picture a staircase with 2^n steps of equal height, from the floor up to just below a ceiling at height V_{ref}. A DAC is told a step number and stands on that step: the number 0 is the floor, the number 1 is one step up, and the largest number 2^n - 1 is the top step. Its output voltage is "step number times step height". Nothing more mysterious happens inside a DAC than turning a number into that height, and the only design question is how to make the heights exact with a handful of resistors. An ADC does the reverse. Someone stands somewhere on a ramp beside the staircase, at a height we do not know, and the ADC must report the step they are standing beside. One honest way is to walk up the stairs one at a time until we pass them (the counter ADC). A faster way is to play "higher or lower": ask whether they are above the middle step, then above the middle of the half that is left, and so on (the successive-approximation ADC). A third way is to post a guard on every step at once and count how many guards see the person above them (the flash ADC). The whole lesson is these three strategies and the staircase they all share. An n-bit DAC with reference voltage V_{ref} maps the code D = b_{n-1}2^{n-1} + \dots + b_1 2 + b_0 (an integer from 0 to 2^n - 1; b_{n-1} is the MSB) to the output V_o = V_{ref}\,\frac{D}{2^n} . The step size (one LSB of output) is \Delta = V_{ref}/2^n: the change in V_o when D grows by 1. The full-scale output is the largest output, all bits 1: V_{FS} = (2^n - 1)\,\Delta = V_{ref}(1 - 2^{-n}). The resolution is the step size, given either in volts (\Delta) or as a fraction of full scale: \Delta / V_{FS} = 1/(2^n - 1), that is 100/(2^n - 1) percent. Some books quote it against V_{ref} instead, \Delta / V_{ref} = 1/2^n; both shrink by half with every extra bit. More bits mean finer steps. Real DACs often have an inverting amplifier at the output, so the circuits below give V_o = -V_{ref}D/2^n (times a gain set by resistors); the magnitude is what the code controls, and we always say which sign a circuit produces. Divide the code by 2^n term by term: \frac{D}{2^n} = b_{n-1}2^{-1} + b_{n-2}2^{-2} + \dots + b_0 2^{-n} = (0.b_{n-1}b_{n-2}\dots b_0)_2 . So V_o = V_{ref} \times 0.b_{n-1}\dots b_0: the code, read as a binary fraction after the point, is the fraction of the reference voltage that appears at the output. The MSB alone contributes V_{ref}/2, the next bit V_{ref}/4, and the LSB V_{ref}/2^n = \Delta. Sanity check. For 4 bits and V_{ref} = 10 V: \Delta = 10/16 = 0.625 V. The code 1000 gives 0.1_2 \times 10 = 5 V (half the reference, as the MSB should); 1111 gives 0.1111_2 \times 10 = (15/16) \times 10 = 9.375 V, which is V_{ref} - \Delta, the full scale. No code reaches 10 V itself, because 0.1111\dots with finitely many 1s is always below 1. For a 4-bit DAC with V_{ref} = 10 V the tempting answer for "the output for 1111" is 10 V. It is 9.375 V: the top step is one step short of the ceiling. The same off-by-one hides in the resolution. Given the full-scale output, the step is V_{FS}/(2^n - 1) (an 8-bit DAC with V_{FS} = 2.55 V has 10 mV steps); given the reference, it is V_{ref}/2^n (V_{ref} = 2.56 V for the same DAC). Dividing 2.55 V by 256 instead of 255 is the expected wrong answer. As a percentage of full scale the resolution is 100/(2^n - 1): 6.67\% for 4 bits, 0.392\% for 8 bits. Some books quote it relative to V_{ref} instead, 100/2^n (6.25\%, 0.391\%); read which one the question means. The real error is to mix them, for example dividing V_{FS} by 2^n. The weighted-resistor DAC An inverting amplifier with a feedback resistor R_f has an input node held at 0 V (a virtual ground): whatever current flows into that node is pushed through R_f, and the output becomes -R_f times the total current. So to build a DAC we only need each bit to deliver a current proportional to its weight. Ohm's law does that for free: connect bit i to the summing node through a resistor, and when the bit is 1 put V_{ref} on the other end. A resistor half as large passes twice the current. Give the MSB the smallest resistor, the next bit twice that, and so on: the currents come out in the ratio 8 : 4 : 2 : 1, exactly the binary weights, and the amplifier adds them. entries.title: Logic families and switch-level circuits
headings: The MOS transistor as a switch
Voltage levels, noise margins, fan-out and power
Worked examples: levels, fan-out and power
entries.text: Optional: beyond the core GATE syllabus. Every gate in Chapters 2 to 6 was a perfect symbol: a 1 went in, a clean 1 came out, instantly and for free. Real gates are built from transistors, and the way they are built decides how fast they are, how much power they burn, how much noise they tolerate and how many other gates they can drive. The current GATE CSE syllabus no longer covers this, but the papers of 1991, 1994 and 1998 did, with four questions in our bank. This lesson treats the MOS transistor as a switch controlled by a voltage, uses that one idea to read pass-transistor networks (the 1991 question) and to design CMOS gates, then turns to the electrical numbers that describe a logic family: voltage levels and noise margins (the 1998 question), fan-out, power and speed, and the comparison of TTL, ECL, CMOS, nMOS and GaAs (the 1994 and 1991 questions). Where this fits Chapter 2, Lesson 1 defined the gates by their truth tables and showed the "switches and a lamp" picture: switches in series behave as AND, in parallel as OR. Here those switches become transistors. The latch of Chapter 6, Lesson 1 reappeared as the SRAM cell in Lesson 1 of this chapter, whose high-impedance memory outputs are exactly the floating node we meet in pass-transistor networks. Lesson 2 of this chapter deals with the other border between digital and analog, the converters. Device physics (how a transistor actually conducts) belongs to an electronics course; we use only what a switch model and a few data-sheet numbers can say. The MOS transistor as a switch Think of a transistor as a water tap whose handle is turned by a voltage. The two ends of the pipe are the transistor's source and drain; the handle is its gate. An NMOS transistor opens when its gate is high (logic 1) and closes when it is low. A PMOS transistor is the opposite: it opens when its gate is low. The tap does not care which way the water flows, so a transistor can pass a signal in either direction between its two ends. There is one catch, and it matters. An NMOS tap is excellent at draining a pipe to the floor (passing a 0) but cannot fill it all the way to the top (it passes only a weakened 1). A PMOS tap is the reverse: it fills to the top perfectly and cannot drain completely. So we say NMOS passes a strong 0, PMOS passes a strong 1, and every circuit in this lesson is designed around that asymmetry. In the switch model a MOS transistor connects its two terminals (source and drain) when it is on and disconnects them when it is off; its gate draws no current. Here V_{tn} and \lvert V_{tp} \rvert are the threshold voltages. With V_{DD} = 5 V and thresholds of 0.7 V (illustrative values, ignoring the body effect), an NMOS passes a 1 as 4.3 V and a PMOS passes a 0 as 0.7 V. A node can be in one of four states: driven 0, driven 1 (strong or degraded), floating (Z: no conducting path to any driven node, so it keeps whatever charge it had, which is not a reliable logic value) or in contention (X: paths to both a 0 and a 1). An NMOS transistor with its gate at V_{DD} pulls a node all the way to 0 V when its other terminal is at 0 V, but raises it only to V_{DD} - V_{tn} when its other terminal is at V_{DD}. For a PMOS with its gate at 0 V the roles of 0 and 1 swap. Idea first: an NMOS conducts only while its gate is more than one threshold above its lower terminal (the source). When it passes a 1, the output itself is that lower terminal, so the transistor switches itself off as the output rises; when it passes a 0, the source is the grounded input and nothing stops the fall. An NMOS conducts while V_{GS} > V_{tn}, where V_{GS} is measured to the source, the terminal at the lower voltage. Passing a 0: the source is the input at 0 V and V_{GS} = V_{DD} > V_{tn} for as long as charge flows, so the output keeps falling until it reaches 0 V. Passing a 1: the output node is now the lower terminal, so it is the source. As it charges, V_{GS} = V_{DD} - V_{out} shrinks; when V_{out} = V_{DD} - V_{tn} the transistor turns off and charging stops. The PMOS argument is the mirror image (it conducts while its gate is more than \lvert V_{tp} \rvert below its higher terminal), so it passes a full 1 and stops a 0 at \lvert V_{tp} \rvert. Put taps in a row and water flows only if every tap is open: series is AND. Put taps side by side and water flows if any of them is open: parallel is OR. A network of transistors between an input and an output is just a plumbing plan, and the question "does the input reach the output?" becomes a Boolean expression in the gate signals. The one new possibility, compared with gates, is that no path may be open at all. Then the output is connected to nothing and simply floats. A pass-transistor network connects signal inputs (not just the supply rails) to an output through transistors whose gates are control signals. Each transistor has a conduction condition: its gate variable g for an NMOS, \overline{g} for a PMOS. A path conducts when every transistor on it is on, and the output is the value of whichever input reaches it. If several paths conduct they must carry the same value, or the node is in contention; if none conducts, the output floats (Z). The 1991 network is of this kind: input x reaches the output f through a PMOS gated by a and then an NMOS gated by b; input y reaches f through an NMOS gated by a and then a PMOS gated by b. For a network built from transistors by series and parallel composition, define its conduction function G: for a single NMOS G = g, for a single PMOS G = \overline{g}; for networks in series G = G_1 G_2; for networks in parallel G = G_1 + G_2. Then the network connects its two terminals exactly when G = 1. Idea first: a chain is connected only if every link holds; a bundle is connected if any strand does. Induction on the construction. A single transistor connects its terminals exactly when it is on, which is g = 1 for NMOS and g = 0 (that is, \overline{g} = 1) for PMOS. Series: the two sub-networks

headings: The idea: sentences with a truth value
Well-formed formulas, precedence and the main connective
Operators defined by a truth table
Try it: the Truth Table Lab
entries.text:
Every proof in this subject, and every "which statement is true" question in GATE, rests on a small machine: statements that are either true or false, five ways of joining them, and a table that says what the joined statement is worth in every situation. This lesson builds that machine carefully. Most of it looks easy, and most of it is, with one exception that costs marks year after year: the implication p 	o q, together with the English phrases that hide it ("only if", "unless", "necessary", "when"). We spend the most time there. Where this fits This is the first lesson of Discrete Mathematics. Lesson 2 uses the truth tables built here to prove laws and decide whether a formula is always true; Lesson 3 uses them to decide whether an argument is valid. Chapter 2 adds quantifiers ("for all", "there exists") on top of the same connectives. If you have done Boolean algebra in Digital Logic, you will recognise \wedge as AND, \vee as OR and 
eg as NOT; the new pieces here are 	o, \leftrightarrow and translation from English. The idea: sentences with a truth value Think of a statement like "it is raining" as a light switch: in any given situation it is either on (true) or off (false), never both, never half. A compound statement such as "it is raining and it is cold" is a little circuit wired from two switches; its light comes on in some situations and not in others. A truth table is simply the list of all situations (every way of setting the switches) with the light's state written next to each. Two facts make this powerful. First, the number of situations is finite: with n switches there are 2^n settings, so we can always check them all. Second, the light depends only on the switches, not on what the sentences mean, so "it is raining and it is cold" and "7 is prime and 4 is even" are the same circuit with different labels. Propositions A proposition is a declarative sentence that is either true (T) or false (F), but not both. Its truth value may be unknown to us, but it must exist. Propositions: "7 is prime" (T), "2 + 2 = 5" (F), "it will rain in Delhi on 1 March 2030" (one of the two, we just do not know which yet). Not propositions: "Close the door." (a command), "Is it raining?" (a question), "x + 1 = 3" (its truth depends on x; it becomes a proposition once x is fixed, or once it is quantified, Chapter 2), "This sentence is false." (it cannot consistently be either). An atomic proposition cannot be split into smaller propositions; we name atoms with letters p, q, r, \dots (propositional variables). A compound proposition is built from atoms with connectives: 
eg (not), \wedge (and), \vee (or), 	o (if … then), \leftrightarrow (if and only if), and sometimes \oplus (exclusive or). A formula built correctly by these rules is a well-formed formula (WFF). "x is a composite number" has no truth value until x is known. GATE 2016 uses such sentences as p, q, r, s and then asks for the x that makes a formula true: the formula is a proposition for each fixed x, and the question is really "for which x is it true". Treat x as a parameter, fix it, and evaluate. The connectives Negation, conjunction and disjunction "p and q" makes a strong claim: it is true only when both parts are true. "p or q" makes a weak claim: it is true as soon as at least one part is true. In logic "or" is always inclusive, so "p or q" is also true when both are true; if you mean "one but not both", you need a different connective, \oplus. "Not p" simply flips the value. p \wedge q is true on exactly one row (both T); p \vee q is false on exactly one row (both F). Rows are listed with T before F, starting from the all-true row; we use this order throughout the subject. "It is raining but it is warm" asserts both parts, so it is r \wedge w. The word "but" adds a note of contrast for the reader, not a different truth table. GATE 2017 hides an "and" in a long sentence the same way. Implication Read p 	o q as a promise: "if you score above 90, then you get a prize." When is the promise broken? Only when you score above 90 and do not get the prize. If you score 85, the promise says nothing about you: whether you get a prize or not, nobody can accuse the speaker of lying. So the promise counts as kept (true) in every case except one: hypothesis true, conclusion false. This is the single most important row in the subject. An implication with a false hypothesis is true ("vacuously true"), however strange the sentence sounds: "if 2 + 2 = 5 then the moon is cheese" is a true implication. p 	o q (read "if p then q", "p implies q") is false only when p is true and q is false: p is the hypothesis (antecedent, premise), q the conclusion (consequent). Equivalently, p 	o q \equiv 
eg p \vee q: "either the hypothesis fails, or the conclusion holds". Compare the two columns row by row. 
eg p \vee q is false only when 
eg p is false and q is false, i.e. when p is T and q is F, which is exactly the one row where p 	o q is false. Two formulas that are false on the same rows (and so true on the same rows) are equivalent. Sanity check: with p = F both are true whatever q is, matching "a false hypothesis keeps the promise". All of these are p 	o q: The key reversal: "p if q" is q 	o p, but "p only if q" is p 	o q. The sentence "p only if q" is true in exactly the situations where p 	o q is true. Idea first: "only if" names a condition that must hold whenever p does. "p only if q" says that p can be true only in situations where q is true. It is violated exactly when p is true while q is false. That is the single false row of p 	o q, and the sentence is not violated on the other three rows (if p is false, nothing has been claimed; if q is true, the condition is met). Same false rows, so the same proposition. "I stay only if you go" is 	ext{stay} 	o 	ext{go}, not 	ext{go} 	o 	ext{stay}. Examiners offer "If you go then I stay" as a distractor; that is the converse. headings: Fast tautology test: try to make it false
Normal forms: DNF, CNF and canonical forms
Try it: the Truth Table Lab
entries.text:
Lesson 1 gave every formula a truth table. This lesson asks the questions GATE actually asks about those tables. Is the column all T (a tautology), all F (a contradiction), or mixed? Do two different formulas have the same column (are they equivalent)? Can we turn one formula into another by algebra instead of by table? Can we write any column in a standard shape (a normal form)? And which small sets of connectives are enough to write every column at all (functional completeness)? This is the single biggest block of propositional logic in GATE: twenty-three previous-year questions, from "which of these is a tautology" (asked in some form almost every few years) to canonical forms, satisfiability of CNF and complete sets of connectives. The good news is that every one of them can be settled by one of three tools: a truth table, a chain of laws, or the "try to make it false" test. We learn all three and, more importantly, learn which one is fastest for which question. Where this fits This lesson builds directly on Lesson 1: you need the truth tables of the five connectives, and especially the fact that p 	o q is false only on the row p = T, q = F. Lesson 3 uses the classification vocabulary from here (valid, satisfiable) to define valid arguments, and its resolution method works on the CNF we build here. Chapter 2 extends the laws to quantifiers. In Digital Logic the same algebra appears as Boolean laws, canonical forms and universal gates; there the emphasis is on circuits and K-maps, here it is on proofs, tautologies and the logic vocabulary GATE uses in the Discrete Mathematics section. Tautologies, contradictions and contingencies Write the truth table of a formula and look only at its final column. There are exactly three things that column can look like. It can be all T: the formula is true in every possible world, whatever the variables mean, so it is a law of logic (like "it is raining or it is not raining"). It can be all F: the formula is false in every world, so it can never happen ("it is raining and it is not raining"). Or it can be mixed: true in some worlds and false in others, so its truth depends on the facts (like "it is raining"). Almost every vocabulary word in this section is a way of saying which of the three pictures you have, or which pictures are ruled out. "Satisfiable" means "at least one T", so it rules out only the all-F picture. "Falsifiable" means "at least one F", so it rules out only the all-T picture. Keep the three pictures in mind and none of the words can confuse you. Let A be a formula and look at its truth-table column. An assignment (row) that makes A true satisfies A (it is a model of A); a row that makes A false falsifies it (it is a counterexample). Every tautology is satisfiable; a contingency is both satisfiable and falsifiable; a contradiction is neither satisfiable nor valid. A is a tautology if and only if 
eg A is a contradiction; A is satisfiable if and only if 
eg A is not a tautology; and A is a contingency if and only if 
eg A is a contingency. Idea first: negation flips every entry of the column, so "all T" becomes "all F" and "mixed" stays "mixed". The column of 
eg A is the column of A with every entry flipped. If A's column has no F, then 
eg A's column has no T: tautology becomes contradiction, and the argument runs backwards too. "A has at least one T" is the same as "
eg A has at least one F", which is "
eg A is not a tautology". A mixed column flips to a mixed column. This is why every "is it valid?" question can be turned into "is the negation satisfiable?", the form a computer (and the falsification test below) uses. For any formulas A, B: If A is a tautology, then A \vee B and B 	o A are tautologies, whatever B is. A \wedge B is a tautology if and only if both A and B are tautologies. If A is a contradiction, then A 	o B is a tautology and A \wedge B is a contradiction. If C 	o D and C 	o 
eg D are both tautologies, then C is a contradiction (unsatisfiable). Substitution: if A is a tautology and we replace a variable everywhere in A by the same formula, the result is still a tautology. Idea first: each fact is a statement about every row, so check one arbitrary row. Take any row. (1) A is T there, and a disjunction with a true part is T; an implication with a true conclusion is T. (2) A \wedge B is T on a row exactly when both are T on it, so "T on every row" holds for the conjunction exactly when it holds for each part. (3) A is F on the row, so A 	o B is 	ext{F} 	o \dots = T, and A \wedge B is F. (4) Suppose some row made C true. Both implications are true on that row, so both D and 
eg D would be true there, which is impossible. So no row makes C true. (5) After substitution, each row gives the replaced variable some truth value; the original A is true for every value of that variable, so the new formula is true on the row too. Sanity check for (4): with C = p \wedge 
eg p both C 	o D and C 	o 
eg D are vacuously true for every D, and indeed C is a contradiction. GATE 1991 is exactly fact (4) with C = F_1 \wedge F_2. A tautology is satisfiable (it is satisfied by every row, so certainly by one). When an option says "satisfiable but not valid", it means "contingency"; when it says "satisfiable", a tautology also qualifies. GATE 2001 offers "F1 is satisfiable, F2 is valid" and "F1 and F2 are both satisfiable": the second is also true but the first is the precise one examiners keyed. Likewise "not a tautology" does not mean "a contradiction": it means at least one F, which includes the contingencies. All T = tautology = valid; all F = contradiction = unsatisfiable; mixed = contingency. Satisfiable = at least one T; falsifiable = at least one F. Negation swaps tautology and contradiction. If C implies both D and

entries.title: Arguments, rules of inference and resolution
headings: Try it: arguments in the Truth Table Lab
entries.text:
The first two lessons taught you to read a formula and to decide what it is worth in every possible world. This lesson turns that skill into reasoning: given some statements we accept (the premises), what else are we forced to accept (the conclusion)? Every proof you will ever write, every "which of the following follows" question in GATE, and every logic-programming engine rests on the same simple test: an argument is good when there is no world in which the premises hold and the conclusion fails. We build that test, then the short-cuts that save you from writing whole truth tables (the rules of inference), the two classic ways of reasoning badly (the fallacies), the single rule that machines use to do all of it (resolution), the vocabulary of axiom systems, and finally the truth-teller and liar puzzles that GATE uses to test whether you can turn a story into a formula. Where this fits Lesson 1 built truth tables and the implication p 	o q; you will use its one false row (T then F) constantly here. Lesson 2 taught tautologies, satisfiability and conjunctive normal form (CNF); validity of an argument is a tautology question in disguise, and resolution works on CNF clauses. Chapter 2 lifts everything in this lesson to predicates and quantifiers: the GATE 1992 question at the end already uses one constant and two variables, and we solve it here by substitution. If you have met SAT solvers or Prolog, resolution is the engine under both. Arguments and validity Think of an argument as a machine that takes true statements in and is supposed to hand a true statement out. A valid machine has a guarantee: whenever everything you feed it is true, what comes out is true. It makes no promise when you feed it something false; garbage in may give garbage out. That is exactly the promise of an implication, from Lesson 1. "If all the premises are true, then the conclusion is true" is broken only in one kind of world: premises all true, conclusion false. So checking validity means hunting for such a world. If the hunt fails in every one of the 2^n worlds, the argument is valid; if it succeeds even once, that world is a counterexample and the argument is invalid, no matter how convincing it sounds. Notice what validity does not care about: whether the premises are actually true today, and what the sentences mean. "If the moon is cheese, then 7 is even; the moon is cheese; so 7 is even" is a valid argument (it has the shape of modus ponens), with a false conclusion, because a premise is false. Validity is a property of the form. An argument is a list of propositions P_1, P_2, \dots, P_n (the premises) together with a proposition C (the conclusion), written P_1, \dots, P_n \;	herefore\; C. The argument is valid if every assignment of truth values that makes all of P_1, \dots, P_n true also makes C true. We then write P_1, \dots, P_n \models C. A row of the truth table on which every premise is true is a critical row. Validity says: the conclusion is true on every critical row. An assignment with all premises true and the conclusion false is a counterexample; an argument is invalid exactly when it has one. A valid argument whose premises are actually true is sound; its conclusion is then true. For premises P_1, \dots, P_n and conclusion C, the following say the same thing: the argument P_1, \dots, P_n \;	herefore\; C is valid; the formula (P_1 \wedge P_2 \wedge \dots \wedge P_n) 	o C is a tautology; the formula P_1 \wedge P_2 \wedge \dots \wedge P_n \wedge 
eg C is unsatisfiable (a contradiction). Idea first: all three statements say "there is no row with every premise true and the conclusion false"; they only phrase it differently. (1 ⇔ 2) Write P = P_1 \wedge \dots \wedge P_n; P is true on a row exactly when every premise is, i.e. on the critical rows. The implication P 	o C is false only on rows where P is T and C is F, i.e. on counterexample rows. So P 	o C is true on every row (a tautology) exactly when there is no counterexample, which is validity. (2 ⇔ 3) 
eg(P 	o C) \equiv P \wedge 
eg C (the negated implication from Lesson 1). A formula is a tautology exactly when its negation is a contradiction, so P 	o C is a tautology exactly when P \wedge 
eg C is unsatisfiable. Sanity check: for p, 
eg p \;	herefore\; q there is no critical row at all (p \wedge 
eg p is never true), so test 3 holds trivially and the argument is valid; test 2 agrees, since (p \wedge 
eg p) 	o q has a false hypothesis on every row. You rarely need all 2^n rows. Start from the only rows that can hurt you: set the conclusion false, which usually fixes one or two variables, then try to make the premises true one by one. Every forced value narrows the search. If you reach a full assignment with every premise true, it is a counterexample: invalid. If every attempt forces some premise to be false, valid. Why it works: a counterexample is precisely "conclusion false, premises true", so searching from the conclusion side searches only the rows that matter. When it fails: when the conclusion is false on many rows (for example a disjunction a \vee b \vee c is false on one pattern only, which is great; but a conjunction a \wedge b is false on three patterns), you must try each pattern; and when several premises are disjunctions you may have to branch. Keep the branches written down, or switch to the full table or to resolution. Examiners like options such as "the conclusion is true, so the argument is valid" or "the conclusion is false, so the argument is invalid". Both reasonings are wrong. A valid argument can have a false conclusion (if a premise is false), and an invalid argument can have a true conclusion by luck. Only the form decides validity: look for a row with true premises and a false conclusion, nothing else. Worked examples: validity Is the argument p 	o q,\ 
eg q \;	herefore\;

eg q: F, T, F, T. The only critical row is p = F, q = F. On FF, 
eg p = T

entries.title: Place value and changing bases
headings: Reading a number in any base
Why every number has one spelling
entries.text: A digit's value depends on where it sits. That one idea, place value, is all you need to read a number written in any base. The big idea Pay ₹347 with notes and coins: 3 hundred-rupee notes, 4 tens, 7 ones. The digit says how many; the position says of what size. Base 2 works the same way, only the bundles are 1, 2, 4, 8, … instead of 1, 10, 100. In base b, the digit in position i (counting from 0 on the right) is worth d_i \cdot b^{\,i}. Every digit must satisfy 0 \le d_i < b. Radix is another word for base. GATE papers use both. Reading a number in any base Add up digit × place value over every position: N = d_k b^k + \dots + d_1 b + d_0 = \sum_{i=0}^{k} d_i\, b^{\,i} Factor out b again and again and the same sum becomes a chain of "multiply, then add": N = \big( \dots ( d_k\, b + d_{k-1} )\, b + \dots \big)\, b + d_0 Convert (1011)_2 to decimal. Write the place value under each digit. \begin{array}{cccc} 1 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 2^3 & 2^2 & 2^1 & 2^0 \\ 8 & 4 & 2 & 1 \end{array} Multiply each digit by its place value. \begin{aligned} 1 \cdot 8 &= 8 \\ 0 \cdot 4 &= 0 \\ 1 \cdot 2 &= 2 \\ 1 \cdot 1 &= 1 \end{aligned} Add the contributions: 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11. (1011)_2 = 11 Convert (257)_8 to decimal. List the place values from the right: 1, 8, 64. Weight each digit. \begin{aligned} 2 \cdot 64 &= 128 \\ 5 \cdot 8 &= 40 \\ 7 \cdot 1 &= 7 \end{aligned} Add: 128 + 40 + 7 = 175. (257)_8 = 175 For which base b is (31)_b = 16? Expand the left side: (31)_b = 3 \cdot b + 1. Solve 3b + 1 = 16, which gives b = 5. Check the digits: 3 < 5 and 1 < 5, so (31)_5 is a valid numeral. b = 5 Why every number has one spelling Every whole number N \ge 0 has exactly one numeral in base b without leading zeros. The last digit is forced: every other term is a multiple of b, so d_0 is the remainder of N \div b. Remove it, divide by b, and the next digit is forced the same way. Repeat until nothing is left. Since no step had a choice, no two numerals can share a value. What is (110)_2 in decimal? 1 \cdot 4 + 1 \cdot 2 + 0 \cdot 1 = 6. Read binary left to right in your head: start at 0; for each bit, double the total and add the bit. For 1011: 0 \to 1 \to 2 \to 5 \to 11. It is the chain form from the derivation. "(19)_8" is not an octal numeral, because 9 is not an octal digit. In equations like (43)_x = (y3)_8 this quietly adds the conditions x > 4 and y < 8, and missing them gives wrong counts. Practice Positions to the right of the point continue the pattern: b^{-1}, b^{-2}, … So (0.1)_2 = \tfrac12. A digit is worth digit × b^{\text{position}}, counting positions from 0 on the right. Every digit must be smaller than the base. To read fast, use the chain: multiply by b, add the next digit.
